Vulnerabilities.Title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with several exploded variables
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, expressions
with several exploded variables (e.g., {+a*,b*}, {+a*,b*,c*},
{/a*,b*}, {?a*,b*}) generate regular expressions vulnerable to
excessive backtracking. A run of members can be divided among the
exploded variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables. When Template#match
or Template#extract is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this
can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial
of service. With 2.9.0, {+a*,b*,c*} takes over 12 seconds to reject
1 KB of input on MRI Ruby 3.2.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only
call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported by Daniel Coles (@manus-pi).
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::URI.normalize_path resolves some paths containing ..
segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs
above the root before any other .. is resolved, the segments that
later .. segments should remove are instead kept:
/../../public/x/../../secret normalizes to /public/x/secret instead
of /secret. URI#normalize, URI#join, URI#== and URI#=== all use
this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable
path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something
that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a
request for a path outside the allowlist.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation,
decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with xn--) that are not
valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when
they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

* labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. xn--google-
  decodes to google;
* labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same
  label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so for
https://xn--google-.example.org/ it displays the host google.example.org,
while #host, #normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
use xn--google-.example.org. An attacker who controls a domain can
therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control.
Applications that compare the result of to_unicode against a list
of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, is not affected. to_ascii and normalized_host
are not affected.

## Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with multiple variables
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates
that put several variables in one expression generate regular
expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than + and # (e.g., {/owner,repo,ref},
   {.a,b}, {a,b,c}, {;a,b,c}). The values are joined by an optional
   separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables
   in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the + or # operators and many variables (e.g.,
   {+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}). A failing match is exponential
   in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g.,
   {+a}{+b}{+c} or {a}{b}{c}), which are polynomial in the input length.

When Template#match or Template#extract is called with a maliciously
crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption,
leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such
as http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref} needs about 2 KB of
input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only
call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with certain exploded expressions
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates
using the * (explode) modifier with the /, ., ;, ? or & operators
(e.g., {/segments*}, {.ext*}, {;params*}, {?query*}) generate
regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When
Template#match or Template#extract is called with a maliciously
crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character,
matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource
consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is
enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as
fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner
between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator,
and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the
operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the
expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported
in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who
only call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported independently by @ebenoist, @andrewstellman, and
then @halogenandtoast.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Denial of service in Addressable URI path normalization
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::URI.normalize_path takes time quadratic in the number
of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., "/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n,
which for n = 3 is /a/a/a/../../../), because it removes one dot
segment per pass over the whole path. URI#normalize, URI#normalized_path,
URI#==, URI#=== and URI#join all call it. Normalizing, comparing or
joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled
resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0,
normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0,
and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and
later. URI.parse by itself is unaffected, as is code that never
normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

## Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem
Security, who also suggested the single-pass approach used in the fix.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning
with xn--) that contain characters which change how text is displayed
without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls
such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width
characters, and other invisible format characters.
Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so it can display a
host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to
a different host. For example, the host of http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/
is displayed as abc, U+202E, moc.com, and the override makes
everything after abc render right to left.

Parsing, host, normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that
show display_uri to users (link previews, chat and email clients,
admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look
like a trusted one.

In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are
decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters
added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

## Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.9.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: json: Ruby JSON: Denial of Service via heap-use-after-free in JSON::ResumableParser
Vulnerabilities.Description: Ruby JSON is a JSON implementation for Ruby. From 2.20.0 until 2.21.2, Ruby's JSON native C extension clears the consumed JSON::ResumableParser input buffer but leaves state.start, state.cursor, and state.end pointing into released storage. When partial_value reconstructs an incomplete object containing duplicate keys, the duplicate-key warning path calls cursor_position, which dereferences those stale pointers. This results in a heap-use-after-free and can terminate the Ruby process. An attacker who can supply JSON stream data to an application using JSON::ResumableParser may cause process termination when the application calls partial_value on incomplete attacker-controlled input containing duplicate object keys. This issue has been fixed in version 2.21.2.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 2.20.0 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: json: Ruby JSON: Denial of service via heap buffer overflow with oversized streamed objects
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Ruby JSON is a JSON implementation for Ruby. Versions 2.9.0 through 2.19.8 are vulnerable to heap buffer overflow when the JSON generator is provided with an oversized streamed object. When streaming to an IO JSON.dump(obj, io) and JSON::State#generate(obj, io) can write past the internal JSON generator buffer when a streamed object contains an
attacker-controlled string near 16 KB. Exploitation would result in a reliable process crash/denial of service. This issue has been fixed in version 2.19.9.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec loads json 2.20.0 (Gemfile-pinned); the flagged 2.9.1 is a stale copy on disk, never loaded at runtime

Vulnerabilities.Title: Possible SSRF on JRuby when resolving external DTDs or entities with `NONET` set
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

On JRuby, the `NONET` parse option did not block an external DTD or entity
whose system identifier used a short-form IPv4 host, such as `http://127.1/`
or `http://169.254.43518/`, or was an absolute path such as `/x.dtd` in a
document parsed from a network URL. An application that parses untrusted XML
with `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or `NOENT` could be made to send network requests,
potentially enabling SSRF.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 applies the `XML::Schema` check from
[GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2):
with `NONET` set, only local resources are loaded.

Only JRuby is affected. Default parse options are not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity (CVSS 3.7).

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later, or do not enable `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or
`NOENT` for untrusted input.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @arpitjain099.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 1.19.4 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Use-After-Free in Nokogiri when replacing an attribute value
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's CRuby native extension could leave a Ruby wrapper pointing to freed
memory when replacing the value of an existing XML attribute via
`Nokogiri::XML::Node#[]=` or `Nokogiri::XML::Node#lang=`. If Ruby code had
already accessed the attribute's child nodes, replacing the value could free
those native child nodes while their wrappers remained reachable. Using one of
those child nodes afterwards could cause an invalid read and a possible
segfault.

This is the same class of issue as
[GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp),
which was fixed for `Attr#value=` in Nokogiri 1.19.4.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 preserves all already-wrapped attribute child nodes before
replacing the attribute value.

JRuby is not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity. Reaching it
requires an unusual API-usage pattern that does not arise during normal use.
The application must directly access an attribute's child nodes and then
replace that same attribute's value via `Node#[]=` or `Node#lang=`. Nokogiri
1.19.5 makes this pattern safe with no change to the public API.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

As a workaround, avoid accessing attribute child nodes directly via
`Attr#children` or similar before replacing the same attribute's value.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by zx (@manus-pi).
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 1.19.4 -- real, unaddressed

Vulnerabilities.Title: Possible Mutation XSS when serializing `noscript` content in `Nokogiri::HTML5` documents
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's HTML5 serializer did not escape text inside `noscript` elements, or
`<` and `>` inside attribute values. When a document parsed with the default
options is serialized, a browser with scripting enabled can parse the output
into markup that Nokogiri's parser never produced. This is a mutation XSS for
applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with `Nokogiri::HTML5`, allow
`noscript` elements, and send the serialized output to browsers.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes both, as the HTML standard's serialization algorithm
requires. Text inside `noscript` is still emitted unescaped for documents
parsed with `parse_noscript_content_as_text: true`.

Only the C extension (CRuby and TruffleRuby) is affected. JRuby does not
implement `Nokogiri::HTML5`.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity (CVSS 2.3,
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`).
Exploitation requires an application that allows `noscript` in sanitized HTML.
Loofah and rails-html-sanitizer do not allow it by default, and Sanitize
always removes it.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

Applications that sanitize HTML and allow `noscript` should parse with
`parse_noscript_content_as_text: true` (available since Nokogiri 1.17.0), or
remove `noscript` elements. This is the workaround for earlier versions, and
it is recommended on every version: some content inside `noscript` is
serialized unchanged, as the standard requires.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @a-zara-n.
Vulnerabilities.ShadowedDetail: bundle exec also loads the flagged 1.19.4 -- real, unaddressed
